title: Weather Is on the List
aliases: A Town That Lasts One Day
logline: A cold upland plain that a colonial government turned into a place to be well in, on the belief that weather and a sound body change how a person moves; at dawn in the coldest weeks the grass is white with frost, and the film holds one blade of it until the sun turns the ice to water. The text being taught says the same thing about weather and health, and files it under the conditions of the sharpest kind of wanting.
human_question: If the weather and the state of my body shape how I want, and not only what I want, is the wanting still mine?

place.what_kind_of_place: A hill station: a high, cold, boggy upland plain at about nineteen hundred metres, ringed by forested mountains, that was made into a health resort by a colonial government in the late 1820s and then grew into a town built to look like somewhere much further north. Its flat valley floor is kept as open turf (a racecourse, a golf course, a park) because the town was laid out around the plain rather than on it, and that open floor is where the cold air pools on still, clear nights. A governor's stone house of the 1820s still stands at its edge, rebuilt over a century into a mock-Tudor hotel. For a few nights each year, mostly in January and February, the temperature on the floor of the plain falls below freezing and the grass is white at dawn. Frost is rare enough on the island to be news every time it comes.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: With the sound off it is a film about cold in a country the viewer thinks of as hot. A white plain at first light, breath visible, gables standing in fog behind the frost; then, very close, ice crystals on grass lit edge-on by the first sun, and one long shot in which the white on a single blade goes clear, beads and runs. It is a nature film at the scale of a centimetre set inside a landscape that looks borrowed from another continent, and it has its own ending: the frost is gone within an hour of sunrise, and the plain is green.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Temperature, and only temperature. The film is built on one hour: the plain is at its coldest just before sunrise, the sun line comes down the western slopes and crosses the valley floor, and wherever it touches, the frost goes. Fog lifts off the turf as it warms. Nothing else is asked to move. There is no drone and the camera itself does not move within a shot.
place.when_it_looks_best: Only on a clear, still morning in the coldest weeks, usually January to early February (frost is recorded between December and April, mainly as ground frost at night). Cloud or wind prevents the frost from forming at all, so the shoot needs a window of several days and a scout the evening before. The best light is the twenty minutes either side of the sun line reaching the valley floor.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: The cold film. Before dawn: an open plain gone white, fog lying on it, the gables of an old house standing in the fog. A close lens on the ground: grass blades furred with ice, a crust of frost on a fallen leaf, breath crossing the frame. Then the sun line arrives across the plain and, in one continuous close shot held in real time, the frost on a blade turns clear, beads and runs, and the blade straightens. By the end the plain is green and ordinary and people are walking across it far off. It is complete without a word: a night's cold and the hour it takes to go. The treatment is its own in the group: dawn, frost, macro on a tripod and locked wides, no drone, no camera movement, and a payoff that is a single shot held in real time rather than a cut or a time-lapse.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The voice makes the same hour into the Pradeepika's list of conditions. In its account of the first kind of wanting, the kind that rises sharply of its own nature, the text lists what helps a mind arise unprompted: a healthy body and mind, patience, practised habit, and getting weather and food as suitable; and it says the prompted kind leaves room for a heaviness. This town exists because men in the nineteenth century believed exactly that weather and a healed body change how a person moves: one of its early books describes a port where everything and everybody seemed enervated (its author blamed trade), and, a year later, a fortnight on this plain that made a fever-wasted man as strong as he had ever been. The film puts the text and the book side by side and then holds the text to its own limits: a condition is not a cause and not a verdict; the list is written of 'a mind', and says nothing about cool air favouring wanting over anything else; and the pleasure of the cold, when it is pleasant, has one seat in the body while everything else that is glad about it is made in the mind. The frost melting is the only demonstration offered: a touch that was painful an hour ago becoming pleasant without anything being added to it.

sequence.on_screen: Pre-dawn, blue light. A locked wide at knee height across an open plain gone white; fog lying a metre deep on it; behind, the gables of an old stone house half drawn in the fog. No movement except breath crossing the bottom of the frame.
sequence.voice: In 1819 an army physician crossed this upland and wrote down the temperature every few hours. Camped in the forest below it the night before, he read fifty-three degrees at five in the morning, and wrote that the air had the frosty feel of a winter night at home. On a morning like this one the plain goes lower still. There is ice on the grass.

sequence.on_screen: Macro, on a tripod at ground level: grass blades furred with ice crystals, lit only by the sky. Then the same lens on a crust of frost on a fallen leaf. Held long enough to see nothing change.
sequence.voice: He also wrote that the wind off the mountains was so cold and piercing it was really disagreeable, and that the travellers held up umbrellas against it. That is a feeling with one seat. The texts count bodily pain in a single kind of mind, the mind of touch, and bodily pleasure in a single kind too. This is where both of them happen.

sequence.on_screen: Locked wide from the edge of the plain as the first sun catches the tops of the forested ridges to the west. The valley floor is still white and in shadow; the old house's windows are dark.
sequence.voice: About nine years later a governor made the plain a place for sick soldiers to get well, and built himself a stone house at its edge. A generation after that, a man who had been wasted by fever was ordered up here. A year before, landing at the island's port, he had written that everything and everybody there seemed enervated, and put it down to trade. Now, he wrote, after a fortnight in this air he was as well and as strong as he had ever been, and he left at once.

sequence.on_screen: Macro again: the sun line visible now as a hard edge of light moving across the frosted turf a few metres away, the near blades still grey.
sequence.voice: The text taught in this series says something close to what that book says, and says it about wanting. Of the kind of wanting that rises sharply on its own, without being pushed, it lists what helps a mind arise that way: a mind and body free of illness, patience, a practised habit, and getting weather and food as suitable. It says the other kind, the kind that has to be urged along, by someone else or by oneself, leaves room for a heaviness, a sluggishness. Weather is on the list.

sequence.on_screen: A slow locked wide: fog lifting off the turf in strips where the sun has reached it, the house's gables clearing, the far half of the plain turning from white to green.
sequence.voice: A list of conditions is not a verdict. The text sets the weather and the body beside patience, habit and company, and none of them decides anything; they make one kind of moment more likely than another. And the list is written of a mind, any mind; it does not say that health or cool air favour wanting over anything else. Nothing about this plain made anyone want anything.

sequence.on_screen: The payoff, one continuous macro shot held in real time, several minutes, no cut: the sun line reaches a single frosted blade; the white goes clear from the tip down, beads into drops, the drops run and the blade lifts.
sequence.voice: One blade, and the sun reaching it.

sequence.on_screen: Close, after the melt: the same blade, wet, in full sun, a drop hanging from its tip. Held.
sequence.voice: Nothing was added to that blade. The cold on it an hour ago would have hurt a hand; the same air now is pleasant on the skin. Pleasant, painful, neither: the texts say there is no fourth way to feel anything, and that only the touch itself happens in the body. What is glad about a morning like this is made in the mind, in more than sixty kinds of moment, many of them good ones. And the texts say plainly that wanting is never unpleasant at the moment it wants, which is why pleasure proves nothing either way.

sequence.on_screen: Final locked wide from the edge of the plain: all green now, the fog gone, the old house plain in sunlight, far off a few figures crossing the turf too small to be anyone.
sequence.voice: The text files this whole list under the mind that wants, and then ranks it strangely: the wanting that comes flat weighs more than the wanting that comes glad, and the wanting that comes with a reason that removes all fault weighs more than the wanting that comes without one. A good reason is not what it means by that. Getting well was a good reason. The plain is only the weather it has always had.

concept_merge.why_together: C006 carries the film: the Pradeepika, in its account of the first greed-rooted mind, gives the background conditions that help 'a mind' arise unprompted, a sound body and mind, patience, practised habit and suitable weather and food [C006-P:L46–L52], says the unprompted mind arises sharply of its own nature [C006-P:L44] and that sluggishness occurs only in the prompted minds [C006-P:L62], and lists freedom from illness among the conditions of the joyful and of the neutral variants alike [C006-P:L29–L31] [C006-P:L76–L78]; the Margaya then ranks neutral over joyful and view-backed over view-free [C006-M:L19]. C032 supplies the only thing a camera can see of any of this, the change of a touch-feeling: bodily pleasure and bodily pain each have one seat, touch-consciousness [C032-P:L99] [C032-P:L103] [C032-M:L7], and nearly all counted gladness is mental [C032-M:L9]. C004 supplies the guard that keeps the film from becoming a sermon against comfort: greed never comes with displeasure [C004-M:L15], and twenty-four of the fifty-four sense-sphere minds are beautiful [C004-P:L27].
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the text and the colonial record share a premise, weather and a healed body change how a mind moves, and draw opposite morals from it: the record treats the cool plain as a cure for a fever-wasted body, and the text lists the same conditions among those that help a mind arise unprompted, in its account of the first kind of wanting. Held together, the three concepts stop either moral from winning. The conditions are tendencies, not fate (C006); the pleasant cold has one seat in the body and the rest is mind (C032); and pleasure is no evidence either way (C004). What is left is the one thing the camera can show honestly: a feeling of touch changing value in front of the lens with nothing added.

concept_links.why: The Pradeepika's first greed-rooted mind is unprompted when it arises 'sharply of its own nature' with no urging [C006-P:L44], and, in the same account, lists what helps 'a mind' arise unprompted: a mind and body kept free of illness, much patience, a good habit in the work, and getting seasons (weather) and food as suitable [C006-P:L46–L52]. The prompted mind, by contrast, leaves room ('අවකාශ') for 'a sluggishness, a heaviness' and sloth-and-torpor occurs only in prompted unwholesome minds [C006-P:L62]. This town was built on the documented belief that the plain's cool climate restores a sick body (a governor's sanatorium for invalid troops; a book crediting 'such a pure and unpolluted air' with a fortnight's cure); the film puts that belief beside the text's list and lets the text's own classification do the work: the same conditions the town was built to supply are, in the text, among what helps a mind arise unprompted, set down in its account of the first kind of wanting. The sentence is written of 'a mind' and does not say the conditions favour wanting over any other kind. Two does_not_transfer lines bind it. 'It's in your genes' or 'it's your destiny': the conditions 'describe tendencies, not fixed fate', so the voice says outright that a list of conditions is not a verdict. And 'Guilt-free pleasure': the view that removes fault makes wanting heavier [C006-M:L19], which is why the last beat separates a true reason (getting well) from what the text means by a view, the excuses of [C006-M:L3] and [C006-P:L33]. Exemption ruling: health is not greed, and the text does not say it is; the sanatorium's founding purpose falls outside any greed-rooted mind as far as the record shows. Whether any visitor's pleasure on the plain was greed-rooted is undecidable and is never judged. 'Wrong view' is not mapped onto anyone.

The Margaya defines greed as the attaching that takes things and people to be good, beautiful, sweet [C004-M:L13] and states that the greed-rooted mind never comes with displeased feeling [C004-M:L15]. That is the line that stops a pleasant morning from being evidence of anything: joy comes with good minds as readily as with greed, so the film never lets the pleasure of the warm sun stand as proof of wanting (does_not_transfer: 'Follow your joy'). And twenty-four of the fifty-four sense-sphere minds are counted beautiful [C004-P:L27], so a film about a place built for comfort must not become a film against comfort (does_not_transfer: 'The sense world is a trap').

Bodily pleasure has one seat, the pleasant touch-consciousness [C032-P:L99], and bodily pain one seat, the painful touch-consciousness [C032-P:L103] [C032-M:L7]; the gladness counted in sixty-two kinds of mind is mental [C032-M:L9], and there is no fourth way of tasting an object [C032-M:L5]. The frost is the only honest image of this the place offers: the physician's 'cold and piercing' wind was a painful touch, and the same air an hour after sunrise is a pleasant one, with nothing added. The Pradeepika's reading that even pleasant feeling is suffering because it depends on conditions and turns [C032-P:L115] [C032-P:L117] is kept out of the voice as a mood: does_not_transfer forbids 'life is suffering' as pessimism and 'pleasure is the enemy', and the group gloss that pleasure is where wanting begins is editorial, not a sentence of the texts.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That the conditions a mind arises in, the weather, the state of the body, are counted by the tradition as shaping how wanting arises, sharp or sluggish, and that this is a list of tendencies rather than a verdict on anyone. That a nineteenth-century town was built on almost the same premise and drew the opposite moral from it. And that the only part of a pleasant morning that happens in the body is the touch; the rest, including whatever is glad about it, is mind.
what_must_be_real: The frost. It is filmed on a morning when it actually forms and is never simulated, sprayed or enhanced, and the melt is shown in real time without speed-ramping. The two historical sentences the voice leans on are quoted from the books as printed: the physician's thermometer readings, frosty air and 'cold and piercing' wind (1821), and the planter-explorer's enervated port and fortnight's recovery (1855). The governor's house is the actual building, with its rebuilding into a hotel acknowledged, not presented as the 1820s house. No person is filmed close enough to be identified, and no guest, racegoer or resident is framed as enjoying, wanting or feeling anything.
position_hint: Early in the group: before the films about taking, owning and spending, this one sets out how the text thinks wanting comes to be sharp or sluggish at all, in a place where the conditions themselves are the subject and no one is accused of anything.
risks: Narrating any historical person's mind. The physician, the governor and the planter-explorer are named only for what they wrote or built. The voice never says what any of them wanted, enjoyed or believed about himself beyond the printed sentence, and the planter-explorer's shooting trips are kept out of the voice altogether, because putting them next to the list of conditions would narrate a man as greedy.

Letting the list of conditions read as fate or as a biological claim. C006's does_not_transfer: the conditions 'describe tendencies, not fixed fate'. The rebirth-mind conditions in the same passages [C006-P:L29] [C006-P:L48] are a traditional claim the digest flags for expert check and are not used.

Turning the film into a sermon against comfort, holidays or the cool climate. C004's does_not_transfer ('The sense world is a trap') and C032's ('Pleasure is where wanting begins, so pleasure is the enemy') both forbid it.
Using the Pradeepika's 'all feeling is suffering' as a mood over the melt. It is a technical analysis, not pessimism (C032 does_not_transfer), and it rests on the Pradeepika alone.

Narrating the colonial climate theory as true, or the text's conditions as observable fact. The voice reports that the book said heat enervated and the air cured, and that the text lists weather and health among conditions; it does not claim that cold sharpens anyone.

Entering land, labour or community history. The upland's later history includes land alienation and plantation labour; none of it is entered, and no living community appears or is described. The physician's note of iron-smelters and gem-seekers crossing the plain is recorded in the historical thread as a correction to 'uninhabited', not narrated as any group's claim.

Death and remembrance. The physician's page records a body on the path of a man who had died trying to cross the mountains to avoid starvation in the aftermath of the 1818 rising; it is excluded completely (bereavement floor, and the rising is conflict history). The legend that a celebrated elephant-hunter was killed by lightning in these hills as a punishment is excluded as kamma-as-fate.

The April season. Horse racing, gambling and the holiday crowds are the town's most-photographed face and are deliberately not filmed or narrated: they would make the film about named people's pleasure and would repeat the racing-ground material proposed for another film in the group.
The frost failing. It forms only on a few clear, still nights a year; a warm or cloudy winter could leave nothing to film. See drop_if.
drop_if: Two consecutive winter windows pass without a filmable ground frost on any accessible open ground in the town's valley floor or the nearby valley bottoms.
Permission to film on the open turf at dawn cannot be obtained from the bodies that manage it, and no public ground with frost can substitute.

An expert reader judges that the Pradeepika's conditions for the unprompted mind [C006-P:L46–L52] cannot bear the weight of a primary-concept film, in which case the location should be re-tested against C006's view and ranking material rather than kept for its frost.
The group's final slate puts a seventh film in this district.

connections.relation: shares a district and a subject with
connections.note: A strict nature reserve a few kilometres away where cloud is the condition that sets each floor of the forest; there the weather decides what can grow, here the text lists the weather among what shapes how a mind wants. Different kind of place (a cloud forest versus a town plain) and deliberately different cinema: that film is an unbroken drone climb, this one has no drone and is shot at ground level. That film also includes frost on grass at two thousand metres, so the frost image is not unique to this film.

The group's seafront lawn, cleared before a fort, raced on and walked on for the air, filmed as one whole day from a single fixed height. Both films touch the colonial belief in air as health; to keep them apart this film does not use racing, the season or promenading at all, and stays with frost, the body and the text's list of conditions.

connections.relation: shares a town and a story with
connections.note: A film confirmed by Chathura on 2026-09-25: the same hill-station town, filmed in the weather it was built for, whose voice names the planter-explorer and tells his fortnight's cure, the barracks for invalids and the twenty houses he found. This film uses the same founding story and the same man's book, unnamed in the voice. The blind GRP-02 selection proposes rewriting IDEA-0018 as a procession film in another district; until that is decided, the two films collide on town, district and history, and one of them must move.

selection.reason: Rebuilt from scratch on 2026-09-26 on the blind GRP-02 selection's proposal, which was tested and kept with corrections. It is the group's only film about the conditions under which wanting arises rather than an act of wanting, and the only one whose payoff is a feeling of touch changing in front of the lens; no other place on the island has a documented founding premise so close to the text's own list.

review.note: This record's body was replaced in full on 2026-09-26 in the blind GRP-02 re-selection; the previous status was already pending, so no confirmation or rejection has been reset, but under standing decision 9 any earlier reading of this record no longer applies. The concepts are unchanged (C006 primary, C004 and C032 supporting). The location is a colonial hill station's frost-prone valley floor, its governor's house of the 1820s and the plain around them, proposed by Claude; the film is shot at dawn in the coldest weeks, with no drone, and pays off on one real-time macro shot of frost melting on a blade of grass. What to judge: whether the Pradeepika's list of conditions for the unprompted greed-rooted mind (health, patience, habit, suitable weather and food) is strong enough to carry a primary-concept film, when the history it meets is a documented nineteenth-century belief that heat enervates and a cool plain restores the body. Corrections made to the proposal: frost falls in December to April and mainly January and February, not in the April season the proposal named; the plain's first written description is John Davy's, from an official tour in August and September 1819, not a hunting party in 1818, and his own page records iron-smelters and gem-seekers crossing the 'uninhabited' plain; Samuel Baker did not found the town (his own book describes an existing station with a governor's house, barracks and about twenty residences) and dates his first visit to 1847. Racing and the April season are left out to keep this film apart from the proposed seafront-lawn film. This takes the district to six films, above the preferred four. Audit 2026-09-26: independent second check. Verdict RECONSIDER, so only factual errors were corrected. The objection is the first half of the test and a collision. The sanatorium story is about bodily health; it does not ask C006's question (how a greed-rooted mind comes to be glad or flat, view-backed or not, prompted or not), and the link rests on one list in the Pradeepika (C006-P:L46-L52) that is written of 'a mind' becoming unprompted, not of wanting alone, so the film joins a place and a doctrine by a shared premise, which is analogy. And the town and its founding story already belong to IDEA-0018, confirmed on 2026-09-25, whose voice names Baker and tells the same fortnight's cure; the slate table puts this district at 8, closed; IDEA-0143 already films frost on grass. Factual fixes: (1) the voice and links said the list favours 'the sharp kind of wanting' and that the same air 'favours the good kinds of mind as much as any other'; the text says the conditions help 'a mind' arise unprompted, in its account of the first greed-rooted mind, and says nothing about good minds; corrected in beats 4 and 5, two_layers, concept_merge and the C006 link; (2) 'carries a heaviness' is 'leaves room for' (අවකාශ) in C006-P:L62; corrected; (3) 'flat and cool' in beat 8 put the weather into C006-M:L19, which ranks neutral feeling, not temperature; now 'flat'; (4) beat 3 spliced Baker: 'enervated' is written of his arrival at the port a year before the fever and blamed on trade ('coffee does not pay'), not on heat, and he does not say he caught the fever in the lowlands; the voice now tells it in order and the record no longer calls it a documented belief that heat enervates; (5) Baker was 'allured' to the island in 1845 and arrived after months of planning, not 'arrived in 1845'; (6) Davy crossed the pattan on his own route after parting from the governor's party partway, not on the tour itself; and beat 1 now says 'this upland', since the identification with the valley floor is disputed in the record's own list; (7) the stale IDEA-0016 connection (a proposal since written as a different film) is replaced by the collision with IDEA-0018, and the IDEA-0025 and IDEA-0143 notes are updated; (8) the district count in the research note is corrected against the slate table. Still unverified: frost on the racecourse turf specifically; any permission or access; the identification of Davy's pattan with the valley floor; Domrös's 1970 paper, which was cited and not checked in the audit.

suggested_location.name: Nuwara Eliya: the open valley floor of the plain (the racecourse and the turf around it), the former Barnes Hall (now the Grand Hotel) at its edge, and the frost hollows of the plain

also_known_as.name: Neuraellyia-pattan
also_known_as.meaning: the name John Davy recorded from his guides in 1819; 'pattan' is an open upland grassland
also_known_as.used_by: Davy, An Account of the Interior of Ceylon (1821)

also_known_as.name: Newera Ellia
also_known_as.used_by: Samuel Baker, Eight Years' Wanderings in Ceylon (1855)

also_known_as.name: Barnes Hall
also_known_as.meaning: Governor Edward Barnes's house of about 1828, rebuilt from the 1890s onward as the Grand Hotel

suggested_location.region: Nuwara Eliya District, Central Province, in the central highlands (verified by reverse geocoding: the racecourse ground and the Grand Hotel both return Nuwara Eliya District)
suggested_location.why_here: The film needs a place whose documented history already argues that weather and the state of the body change how a person moves, because that is the Pradeepika's claim about the unprompted greed-rooted mind [C006-P:L46–L52], and it needs that argument to be photographable. This plain is both. It was made a sanatorium in the late 1820s; its most influential early book (Baker, 1855) calls the port 'enervated' on arrival (blaming trade: 'coffee does not pay') and, a year later in the story, credits the plain's air with a fortnight's cure of a fever-wasted man; and the plain's own physical signature, rare on the island, is the cold itself: ground frost on the valley floor on still, clear nights in the coldest weeks. The frost is also the only honest image the place offers of C032's single seat of bodily pleasure and pain [C032-P:L99] [C032-P:L103]: a touch that is painful at dawn and pleasant an hour later with nothing added.

historical_thread.story: The first written description of the plain is John Davy's. An army physician attached to Governor Sir Robert Brownrigg, he left Colombo with the governor's party on 21 August 1819, parted from it at Ruwanwella, travelled on by his own route through Kotmale, and on the way to Fort Macdonald, before rejoining the suite at Maturatta, crossed a great open upland 'our guides called Neuraellyia-pattan', which he estimated at fifteen or twenty miles in circumference and about 5,300 feet above sea level. He recorded its temperature repeatedly (53°F at 5 a.m. at the camp below it, not above 62°F in full noon sun on the plain), wrote that the fires, the starlight 'and the frosty feel of the air, reminded me of a winter-night in England', that the wind off the mountains was 'so cold and piercing, that it was really disagreeable', and that the region, 'possessing, in all probability, a fine climate, (certainly a cool climate)', was 'quite deserted by man', the dominion of elephants. On the same page he records that his guides said the plain was visited only by the blacksmiths of Kotmale, who came in the dry season to make iron, and by the gem-renter and his people. His book was published in 1821. Governor Sir Edward Barnes (in office 1824–1831) made the plain a sanatorium, opened the road to it and on to Badulla, built barracks and officers' quarters for invalid troops, and built himself a stone house, Barnes Hall, at a cost Baker reports as 'it is said, 8000l'. Secondary accounts date the house to 1828 and the sanatorium to 1828 or 1829. Samuel Baker, later the explorer of the upper Nile, wrote that it was in 1845 that 'the spirit of wandering allured me towards Ceylon'; he arrived after months of planning and, at the end of twelve months of shooting, fell ill with 'jungle fever'. In Eight Years' Wanderings in Ceylon (1855) he wrote that his doctor ordered him to 'the sanitarium of the island'; that the port where he first landed had 'a peculiar dulness', 'a sort of something which seemed to say, "coffee does not pay"', where 'everything and everybody seemed enervated' (written of his arrival, a year before the fever); and that 'at the expiration of a fortnight' on the plain 'I was as well and as strong as I ever had been; and in proof of this I started instanter for another shooting excursion'. He dated his first visit to 1847, found the station neglected after Barnes (about twenty private residences, barracks, a rest-house and a bazaar of about two hundred people), bought land from the government at twenty shillings an acre, and in 1848 brought out a party of settlers, cattle, sheep, a thoroughbred stallion and a pack of foxhounds, meaning, in his words, to make residence there 'something approaching to a country life in England'. Barnes Hall later became a guest house and, from 1892, the Grand Hotel, rebuilt in stages until the 1930s gave it its mock-Tudor front. Horse racing on the plain dates from a Gymkhana Club meeting of 1875, and an April holiday season grew around it. The frost is measured: Manfred Domrös's study of frost in Ceylon (1970) counts it as occurring at Nuwara Eliya, and the island's lowest recorded temperatures, below freezing, are from this station in January and February.
historical_thread.how_it_binds: C006 asks how a greed-rooted mind comes to be glad or flat, view-backed or view-free, sharp or urged along, and the Pradeepika answers with background conditions: freedom from illness for the joyful mind [C006-P:L29–L31] and for the neutral one [C006-P:L76–L78]; a healthy mind and body, patience, practised habit and suitable weather and food for the unprompted one, which arises 'sharply of its own nature' [C006-P:L44] [C006-P:L46–L52]; and a heaviness, sluggishness, only in the prompted [C006-P:L62]. The written history of this plain is a sustained argument on exactly that premise, weather and a healed body change how a person moves, made by the people who built the place: a governor's sanatorium for invalid troops, and a book that calls the port enervated on arrival and, a year later in its story, credits the plain's air with a fortnight's cure. The doctrine and the document share the premise and part company on its meaning; the record calls the result health, the text lists the same conditions among what helps a mind arise unprompted, in its account of the first kind of wanting. The film does not choose between them. It holds the text to its own limit (C006's does_not_transfer: the conditions are tendencies, not fate), keeps every person's mind out of the voice, and gives the camera the one thing it can honestly see, a touch-feeling changing value with the temperature [C032-P:L99] [C032-P:L103].
what_is_certain: John Davy crossed an upland his guides called 'Neuraellyia-pattan' on a route of his own during Governor Brownrigg's tour of August–September 1819 (between parting from the party at Ruwanwella and rejoining it at Maturatta) and described it in An Account of the Interior of Ceylon (1821), pp. 457–460, with thermometer readings, 'the frosty feel of the air', a wind 'so cold and piercing, that it was really disagreeable', and the phrase 'quite deserted by man'.

On the same pages Davy records that the plain was visited by the blacksmiths of Kotmale, who came in the dry season to make iron, and by the gem-renter and his people; he also found sapphire recorded 'on the Neuraellyia patan' (p. 23).

Samuel Baker, Eight Years' Wanderings in Ceylon (1855), ch. I: the port where 'everything and everybody seemed enervated', described on his arrival and put down to trade ('coffee does not pay'), a year before the fever; his doctor's order to go to 'the sanitarium of the island'; recovery in a fortnight to 'as well and as strong as I ever had been'; Barnes's stone house, road and barracks for invalids; 'Upon my first visit to Newera Ellia in 1847'.
Baker's settlement party (emigrants, livestock and foxhounds) sailed from London in September 1848; he bought land from the government at twenty shillings an acre (Baker 1855, ch. I–II).

Barnes was Governor of Ceylon 1824–1831; after his departure his house was let to his successor Wilmot-Horton, later became a guest house, and was sold in April 1892 to the Nuwara Eliya Hotels Company as the Grand Hotel, with extensions in the 1890s, 1904 and the 1930s (Wikipedia, Grand Hotel).

Ground frost occurs at Nuwara Eliya on a few nights a year, mainly January–February (Domrös, 'Frost in Ceylon', Archiv für Meteorologie, Geophysik und Bioklimatologie B 18, 1970; Sunday Times, 14 January 2018, reporting 3.6°C on 6 January 2018 and frost in the surrounding valleys).
The racecourse ground and the Grand Hotel both reverse-geocode to Nuwara Eliya District, Central Province (OpenStreetMap Nominatim).

Baker (1855, ch. I) dates his interest in the island to 1845 ('It was in the year 1845 that the spirit of wandering allured me towards Ceylon') and his fever to the end of twelve months of shooting trips; he does not say where the fever was caught.
what_is_disputed: Who 'discovered' the plain and when. Popular accounts say John Davy found it on a hunting party in 1818. Davy's own book places his crossing on an official tour that left Colombo on 21 August 1819, and describes no hunt. Some accounts credit unnamed British officers lost while elephant-hunting in 1818; no primary source for that was reached. Both years stay in the record; the 1819 crossing is the earliest attestation actually read.

'Uninhabited'. Davy calls the plain 'quite deserted by man' and in the next paragraph records smiths and gem-seekers using it seasonally, and supposes it was once cleared. Absence of houses is not absence of use; the film does not use the word 'discovered'.

Whether Davy's 'Neuraellyia-pattan' is the town's valley floor itself or the wider upland of which it is a part; his route (from the Kotmale side toward Fort Macdonald) crosses the upland, and the identification with the present racecourse plain is not exact.
The date of the sanatorium and of Barnes Hall: 1828 in most secondary accounts, 1829 in some; Baker (1855) gives no year.

Who founded the town. Wikipedia says Samuel Baker founded it in 1846. Baker's own book describes an existing station of Barnes's making, dates his first visit to 1847 and his settlement to 1848; 'founded by Baker' is contradicted by the founder-figure's own account.

The racing chronology is inconsistent on its own terms in one widely used source: the Governor's Cup is said to have been 'first contested in 1833' while the first race meeting is dated 1875. Not used in the film.

Whether frost forms on the racecourse turf itself on any given year: widely reported for the town and for nearby valley bottoms (the Sunday Times names Meepilimana, Kandapola, Ragala and others), but no source was found that names the racecourse or golf course specifically. A scout is required.

what_to_film: Pre-dawn locked wides at knee height across the white valley floor, fog lying on it, the old house's gables in the fog behind (35 mm, tripod).
Ground-level macro (100 mm) on frosted grass blades, frost on fallen leaves and on fence rails, lit by the sky before sunrise.
The sun line coming down the western ridges and crossing the valley floor, filmed as a locked wide.
The payoff: one continuous real-time macro shot of a single frosted blade as the sun reaches it, held from white to wet, several minutes, no cut, no speed change.
Fog lifting off the turf in strips; the plain turning from white to green; the house clearing in sunlight.
Sound: the plain at dawn only (wind, birds, a distant town waking). No music, no frost-crunch foley, no voices.
suggested_location.access: The valley floor is in the town and reached by road. The racecourse ground is state-owned (managed since 2011 by the Sugathadasa National Sports Complex Authority, with meetings run by the Sri Lanka Turf Club, per Wikipedia) and dawn access needs their permission; the golf course is a private club; the Grand Hotel is private and its frontage should be filmed from public ground or with the hotel's consent. If none of these grounds gives frost or permission, the frost hollows in the valley bottoms named in press reports around the town are the substitute and need landowners' consent. No drone is planned, so no civil aviation clearance is needed. Desk research only; nothing verified on the ground.
suggested_location.best_time: A clear, windless morning in January or early February, from about 05:00 until an hour after the sun reaches the valley floor. Frost has been recorded from December to April but mainly in the coldest weeks. Avoid the April season entirely (crowds, and no frost). Allow a window of a week and scout each evening for clear sky.

suggested_location.research_note: Desk research, 2026-09-26, done blind to this record's earlier body. The two primary texts (Davy 1821, Baker 1855) were downloaded from the Internet Archive and searched; every quotation in this record is from them as printed. Corrections to the blind proposal: (1) it placed the frost shoot in April; frost at this station falls mainly in January and February, and April is the warm holiday season, so the shoot moves to January–February; (2) it cited Davy's 1821 book as unread and the 'discovery' as 1818 or 1819: the book records an official tour leaving Colombo on 21 August 1819, not a hunting party, and records seasonal users of the 'deserted' plain; (3) Wikipedia's 'founded by Samuel Baker in 1846' is contradicted by Baker's own dating of his first visit (1847) and his description of an existing station. The proposal's racecourse, gambling and April season material was dropped from the film to keep it apart from the proposed seafront-lawn film in the same group, which also turns on colonial racing and 'the air'. District budget: Nuwara Eliya held five films outside GRP-02 and GRP-03; this takes it to six, above the preferred four and one short of closed. The reason is that no other district has a documented founding premise matching the text's list of conditions, and the frost is unique to this station. GRP-03's blind selection was not available when this was written; if it also places a film here the district reaches seven and one of the two must move. Frost on the racecourse turf specifically could not be confirmed from any source and must be scouted; access, permissions and the ground's management are unverified. Images: four files confirmed to exist on Commons via the imageinfo API; two are not the filming frame and are captioned so. Audit 2026-09-26: the district count above is out of date. The generated slate table now shows Nuwara Eliya at 8 films with this one, closed; it includes IDEA-0018, a film already confirmed by Chathura on 2026-09-25, set in this same town, whose voice names Baker and tells his fortnight's cure, and IDEA-0143 at Hakgala, which also films frost on grass. The blind GRP-02 selection proposes moving IDEA-0018 elsewhere; until that is decided this film duplicates its town and its central historical story. Davy's route was re-read: he parted from the governor at Ruwanwella and crossed the pattan on his own way to Fort Macdonald. Baker's 'enervated' is written of his arrival at the port and blamed on trade, not climate; the record no longer calls it a documented belief that heat enervates.

unknowns: Whether ground frost forms on the racecourse or golf turf, rather than only in the outlying valley bottoms, in a given winter.
Permission for dawn access to the racecourse ground and the hotel frontage.
Whether an expert reader accepts the Pradeepika's list of conditions for the unprompted mind as enough to carry C006 as primary.
The exact identity of the part of the upland Davy crossed in 1819 with the present valley floor.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location was proposed by Claude and awaits Chathura's review; it has not been confirmed. Quotations from Davy (1821) and Baker (1855) are documentary and were read in the printed texts; the frost climatology is from a published study and press reports; everything about access, permission and filming conditions is desk research and unverified. No scene or shot has been filmed.
